This notebook backs the "Hourly marginal distribution costs" methods section of the CT
Eversource rate report (`index.qmd`). The distribution and sub-transmission marginal cost
schedule allocates an annualized $/kW-year cost across the **top 100 load hours** of the
ISO-NE Connecticut load zone. That allocation depends on which calendar year's load we rank,
so here we re-run the peak-hour selection for several load years and ask: **in which months
do the top 100 hours fall, and how much does that shift from year to year?**

The outputs are report variables — the share of peak hours by month for each load year —
which `index.qmd` reads directly so the table there is never hardcoded.

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: setup

from __future__ import annotations

import pickle
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT

from lib.great_tables import get_switchbox_gt_tab_options
from lib.format import pct
from lib.quarto import display_gt

report_vars: dict = {}
```

## Parameters

The production schedule uses load year 2025 and the top 100 hours. We test the four most
recent complete-or-current calendar years of ISO-NE zone load.

```{python}
#| label: params

ZONE = "CT"
LOAD_YEARS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
N_PEAK_HOURS = 100
PRODUCTION_LOAD_YEAR = 2025

PATH_ZONE_LOADS = "s3://data.sb/isone/hourly_demand/zones"
S3_OPTS = {"aws_region": "us-west-2"}

MONTH_ABBR = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]

report_vars["load_years"] = LOAD_YEARS
report_vars["n_peak_hours"] = N_PEAK_HOURS
report_vars["production_load_year"] = PRODUCTION_LOAD_YEAR
```

## Import data

ISO-NE publishes hourly real-time demand by load zone. Each row is one hour for one zone;
`interval_start_et` is the hour beginning, in Eastern time, and `load_mw` is the zone's
average load over that hour. The CT zone covers both Eversource and United Illuminating
service territory.

```{python}
#| label: load-zone-loads

zone_load = (
    pl.scan_parquet(f"{PATH_ZONE_LOADS}/zone={ZONE}/", storage_options=S3_OPTS)
    .filter(pl.col("year").is_in(LOAD_YEARS))
    .select("year", "interval_start_et", "load_mw")
    .rename({"interval_start_et": "timestamp"})
    .collect()
)

zone_load.head()
```

Let's check we have a full year of hours for each load year. The counts differ slightly from
8,760 because of the leap day in 2024 and because ISO-NE's Eastern-time timestamps repeat one
hour in November (DST fall-back) and skip one in March (spring-forward).

```{python}
#| label: check-hour-counts

zone_load.group_by("year").agg(pl.len().alias("n_hours")).sort("year")
```

## Data preparation

The fall-back hour appears twice with the same wall-clock timestamp. We collapse duplicates
to their mean so each timestamp is a single hour, matching how the production pipeline
normalizes the series before ranking. The skipped spring-forward hour is left missing — it is
a March hour and cannot be in the summer top 100.

```{python}
#| label: dedupe-timestamps

zone_load = (
    zone_load.group_by("year", "timestamp")
    .agg(pl.col("load_mw").mean())
    .sort("year", "timestamp")
)

assert zone_load.group_by("year").len().filter(pl.col("len") < 8759).is_empty()
```

## Peak-hour selection by load year

For each load year, we rank hours by load and keep the top `{python} N_PEAK_HOURS`. Then we
count how many of those hours fall in each calendar month and convert to a share of the
peak-hour set.

```{python}
#| label: peak-hours-by-month

peak_hours = (
    zone_load.with_columns(
        pl.col("load_mw").rank(method="ordinal", descending=True).over("year").alias("rank")
    )
    .filter(pl.col("rank") <= N_PEAK_HOURS)
    .with_columns(pl.col("timestamp").dt.month().alias("month"))
)

peak_share_by_month = (
    peak_hours.group_by("year", "month")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("n_hours"))
    .with_columns((pl.col("n_hours") / N_PEAK_HOURS).alias("share"))
    .sort("year", "month")
)

peak_share_by_month
```

The report table shows every month that contains at least one peak hour in any load year, so
its columns come from the data rather than a fixed summer window. We record which months those
are, and which month carries peak hours in every load year (the one the narrative quotes a
range for).

```{python}
#| label: check-summer-only

PEAK_MONTHS = sorted(peak_share_by_month["month"].unique().to_list())

_months_every_year = (
    peak_share_by_month.group_by("month")
    .agg(pl.col("year").n_unique().alias("n_years"))
    .filter(pl.col("n_years") == len(LOAD_YEARS))
    .sort("month")["month"]
    .to_list()
)
assert len(_months_every_year) == 1, _months_every_year
ALWAYS_PEAK_MONTH = _months_every_year[0]
```

Now pivot to one row per load year, one column per month, filling months with no peak hours
as zero.

```{python}
#| label: peak-share-table

PEAK_MONTH_COLS = [MONTH_ABBR[m - 1] for m in PEAK_MONTHS]

peak_share_wide = (
    peak_share_by_month.pivot(values="share", index="year", on="month", sort_columns=True)
    .fill_null(0.0)
    .sort("year")
)
# Pivot names columns by month number; relabel and add any summer month with no peak hours.
peak_share_wide = peak_share_wide.rename(
    {c: MONTH_ABBR[int(c) - 1] for c in peak_share_wide.columns if c != "year"}
)
peak_share_wide = peak_share_wide.with_columns(
    [pl.lit(0.0).alias(c) for c in PEAK_MONTH_COLS if c not in peak_share_wide.columns]
).select("year", *PEAK_MONTH_COLS)

peak_share_wide
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-peak-hour-share-by-month
#| tbl-cap: "Share of top-100 peak hours by month, ISO-NE Connecticut zone, by load year."

_gt = (
    GT(peak_share_wide)
    .cols_label(year="Load year")
    .fmt_percent(columns=PEAK_MONTH_COLS, decimals=0)
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(_gt)
```

## Report variables

`index.qmd` renders this table in markdown with inline values, so we export the shares as a
nested dict keyed by load year then month abbreviation, plus the column order and the share
range for the one month that has peak hours in every load year.

```{python}
#| label: report-vars

peak_month_share: dict[int, dict[str, float]] = {
    int(row["year"]): {c: float(row[c]) for c in PEAK_MONTH_COLS}
    for row in peak_share_wide.iter_rows(named=True)
}
report_vars["peak_month_share"] = peak_month_share
report_vars["peak_month_cols"] = PEAK_MONTH_COLS

# The one month with peak hours in every load year, and its share range.
_always = MONTH_ABBR[ALWAYS_PEAK_MONTH - 1]
report_vars["always_peak_month"] = _always
_shares = [s[_always] for s in peak_month_share.values()]
report_vars["always_peak_month_share_min"] = min(_shares)
report_vars["always_peak_month_share_max"] = max(_shares)

# Which months the production load year's peak hours fall in (for the Step 3 prose).
report_vars["production_peak_months"] = [
    m for m, s in peak_month_share[PRODUCTION_LOAD_YEAR].items() if s > 0
]

# Preformatted cell text per load year, in column order, so index.qmd's table needs no
# formatting of its own.
report_vars["peak_share_cells"] = {
    year: [pct(shares[m]) for m in PEAK_MONTH_COLS] for year, shares in peak_month_share.items()
}

report_vars
```

## Export report variables

```{python}
#| label: export-report-vars

Path("../cache").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Path("../cache/marginal_costs_vars.pkl").write_bytes(pickle.dumps(report_vars))
```
